passages.title: A Night at the Debate
passages.text:
Last month my uncle Hung, a retired teacher, watched a televised debate between two candidates, and he has been talking about it ever since. Hung is a **sensible** man who rarely loses his temper, so I was surprised when he called one **politician** "completely **silly**" after the man promised free petrol for everyone. "Nobody could pay for that," Hung said. The other candidate was no better. Her speech was so **confusing** that even the presenter asked her to explain the figures again. Many viewers felt **confused**, and some phoned the studio to complain that the numbers seemed to change every minute. Journalists say that some speakers **confuse** voters on purpose, because people who cannot follow an argument are less likely to challenge it.

The most striking moment came at the end. A young woman in the audience described how her father had lost his job, and she began to **get emotional** as she spoke. The room fell quiet. Hung admitted that he is not usually an **emotional** person, but that night he had tears in his eyes. "Politics is about real lives," he told me. "Clear answers matter more than clever slogans."

passages.title: My Sister's Prize
passages.text:
When my younger sister Lan started school, she was a **cheerful** child who greeted everyone on the bus. I, on the other hand, was a **curious** teenager who spent most evenings reading about how machines work. My **curiosity** often got me into trouble, and my parents sometimes found a radio in pieces on the kitchen floor.

Things changed when Lan won a drawing prize. Everyone praised her, and I felt **jealous** of the attention she received. I watched her **jealously** as our grandmother hung her picture on the wall, and I refused to say well done. The **jealousy** grew until I felt **miserable**: I could not enjoy my meals, and I stopped speaking to her.

One night, Lan knocked on my door and **curiously** looked at the broken radio on my desk. "Can you teach me how it works?" she asked. Her simple question made me ashamed. We spent the whole evening repairing the radio together, and by midnight I was laughing again. Looking back, I realise that envy only hurt me, while sharing my hobby made us closer than ever.

passages.title: Student Mental Health
passages.text:
According to a recent health survey, one in five university students may **suffer from** a mental health problem. Doctors use the term **mental disorders** to describe conditions that affect how people think, feel and behave. A **disorder** is not simply a bad mood; it lasts for weeks or months and interferes with daily life.

Several types are common among young adults. Students with **sleep disorders**, such as insomnia, are exhausted during lectures. Those with **anxiety disorders** feel constant worry and sometimes panic before exams. Others with **eating disorders** are led to skip meals or eat in unhealthy ways because they are afraid of gaining weight. Often, these problems appear together.

Long periods of stress and loneliness can **depress** even a strong person. A student who feels **depressed** may lose interest in friends, stop attending class and find it hard to get out of bed. Experts stress that these illnesses can be treated. They urge universities to provide counselling services, and they advise anyone who is worried to talk to a doctor early rather than wait until the situation becomes serious.

passages.title: A Grandmother's New Start
passages.text:
After my grandfather died, my grandmother became a **widow** at the age of sixty. The first winter was **depressing**: the house was silent, and she rarely left her chair. Her doctor explained that she was suffering from **depression**, a real illness rather than simple sadness. At first she refused help, but my aunt Lan persuaded her to join a walking club.

Now she walks **energetically** every morning and has made many new friends. She says she used to **be frightened of** meeting strangers, yet today she can **get on well with** almost anyone in the club.

Her own life story is interesting too. She **got married** at nineteen to a young teacher from a village near Hue. Years later, a legal **dispute** over land with a neighbour nearly divided the family, but my grandfather solved it peacefully by speaking to a lawyer instead of shouting.

I admire her courage. Many older people feel ashamed to talk about their feelings, but she has shown us that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

passages.title: A Wedding in London
passages.text:
Last summer my cousin Mai travelled to London to **get married to** an English engineer named Tom. Her grandmother, who **married** a sailor in 1960, had always dreamed of seeing this day. Sadly, a small **tragedy** nearly spoiled the trip: Mai's suitcase, with her wedding dress inside, was lost at the airport. Luckily the airline found it two days later.

Before the wedding, our family had to change some money. The official **currency** of the United Kingdom is the pound, often called **sterling**. At the bank, the clerk handed me a crisp twenty-pound **note** and explained that smaller amounts come as a **coin**, such as a one-pound or two-pound piece. I kept one as a souvenir.

The ceremony itself was calm and emotional, with many guests in tears. At the evening reception, however, the music became louder and the dancing began to **get wild**. Even my shy uncle joined in. At midnight Tom's father gave a speech, welcoming our relatives and promising to visit Vietnam next year. It was one of the happiest trips of my life, and a memory that our whole family will treasure.

passages.title: Money Matters at University
passages.text:
Starting university is exciting, but it is also expensive. Many students **get a loan** to cover their costs, and in Britain the most common type is the **student loan**, which is repaid only after graduation. When the first payment arrives, you must **pay your fees** before the deadline, or the university may stop you from joining your course.

Managing daily money is another challenge. Most banks advise young people to check their balance every week, because you want to **be in credit** rather than overdrawn at the end of the month. If you need cash, you can **take out money** at a **cashpoint** near the library; Americans call the same machine **a cash machine**.

Be careful, though. Small purchases add up quickly, and some students end up having to **owe money** to their friends after a night out. A simple budget helps a great deal. Write down what you receive each month, list your regular costs, and keep a small amount for emergencies. After a few weeks, spending wisely becomes a habit, and you will feel much less stressed about your future.

passages.title: A Student's First Rent
passages.text:
When I started university in Hanoi, I quickly learned that living alone is expensive. Every month I **pay rent** for a small room near campus, and the landlord also asked me to **pay a deposit** equal to **one month's rent** before I moved in. That was a large **amount of money** for a student, and my parents could only help a little. I had never handled so many bills before, so I made a simple budget in my notebook and wrote down everything I spent on food, transport and books.

I really wanted a new laptop, but I **can't afford** one yet. So I decided to **save up for** it by working at a café at weekends. In the meantime, I **borrow** a laptop **from** my cousin Lan, who hardly ever uses hers. My uncle also helped me with the deposit, and I promised to **pay back money** he had given me, bit by bit, starting next month. Although money is tight, I am proud that I am learning to manage my own life. Every small coin I keep now feels like a step towards independence.

passages.title: First Aid at Summer Camp
passages.text:
Last summer I joined a school camp in the mountains as a volunteer helper. On the first evening, our leader, Mr Hung, gathered the children and gave them simple safety rules. "If you **cut yourself**, tell an adult immediately," he said. "Never hide a small injury."

That advice proved useful on the second day. A boy named Tuan fell while playing football, and his knee began to **bleed**. Mr Hung cleaned the wound and **put a bandage around** it, then smiled and told Tuan to rest. Tuan's friend Bao kindly offered to **lend** him a cap to keep the sun off his face.

Later that night, a girl called Mai said she would **feel sick** after eating too quickly. Her face was pale, and she held her stomach. The camp nurse asked her to **take some tablets** with a glass of water, and Mr Hung decided to **give** her **some medicine** for the stomach as well. He explained that if she still felt unwell in the morning, they would drive her into town to **see a doctor**. Fortunately, Mai slept well and woke up smiling. The children learned that small accidents are not frightening when adults stay calm.

passages.text:
My grandfather smoked for forty years, and last winter his health became a serious worry for our family. At first he only complained about a dull **ache** in his chest and thought it was nothing. I offered to **go to the chemist** and buy him some cream. The pharmacist listened carefully and explained that people who **suffer from** breathing problems should be checked quickly, so she advised us not to wait.

Grandfather ignored her advice for several days. His cough grew worse, and it began to **hurt** whenever he breathed deeply. Soon even walking up the stairs was **painful**. At last my father insisted that he **go into hospital** for tests.

The results shocked us all. The doctors found **lung cancer**, and a few weeks later he also had a mild **heart attack**, which frightened the whole family. Fortunately, the medical team acted fast and he recovered well enough to start treatment. Today he is much stronger, and he has given up smoking for good. He often tells young people to listen to their bodies and not to delay when something feels wrong.

passages.text:
Last Saturday I visited a busy market with my aunt, who is famous for finding bargains. "Prices are never fixed here," she explained. "If you smile and stay patient, a seller is more **likely** to listen to you."

At the first stall, a pile of silk scarves seemed to **be on special offer**, and a sign promised "**three for the price of two**". My aunt was not satisfied with that, however. She wanted to **haggle**, which made me nervous, because I had always paid the price on the label.

For ten minutes she and the seller were happily trying to **haggle over the price** of one scarf in particular. He sighed, laughed and shook his head, but in the end they managed to **agree a lower price**. I walked away with three scarves for much less than I had expected.

At home I noticed a small hole in one of them. My aunt was calm. The seller had a clear policy, she said, so I would **be likely to** get a **refund** if I returned it within a week. Bargaining, I realised, is a skill that anyone can learn.

passages.title: A Tense Day at the Office
passages.text:
Last week our team had a **tense meeting**. Our manager, Mr Hung, was unhappy because Tuan had handed in an unfinished report. Tuan replied that checking the figures was not part of his **job description**, and the argument grew louder.

**In the heat of the moment**, Mr Hung **raised his voice at** Tuan. "This is the **absolute last time** I will accept a late report!" he shouted. Everyone stared at their laptops. Tuan's face turned red, because being criticised **in front of people** is humiliating for anyone.

The next morning, Mr Hung asked Tuan to come to his office for a **one-on-one** talk. He admitted that he had been unfair and said he wished he could **take back** his harsh words. Tuan explained that he had been given too many tasks, and that nobody had told him the deadline had moved.

They agreed to review his duties together and rewrite the description so that it was clear. Later, several colleagues told me that the manager's honesty had earned him more respect than his anger ever had.

passages.title: Talking Like Adults
passages.text:
Last month I decided to **address** my flatmate Minh **about** the kitchen. The night before, he had left **raw meat** on the counter for hours while he cooked a large pot of **barley** soup. Worse, he had been so excited about buying a **certificate of deposit** with his bonus that he forgot everything else.

At first I was angry and wanted to shout. Then I told myself it would be better to **have a conversation like adults**. I waited until he had finished dinner and said quietly, "We need to talk about food safety."

To my surprise, Minh listened carefully. He did not make excuses and instead chose to **apologize for his behavior**. "I should **be mature enough to** admit my mistakes," he said. He promised to wrap and store meat properly and to clean the counter every evening.

I smiled. "That is fine **as long as it doesn't happen again**," I replied. Since then the kitchen has stayed spotless, and our friendship feels stronger than before.

passages.title: A Sunday Walk with Grandfather
passages.text:
Every Sunday morning, my grandfather and I walk along the **footpath** that runs beside the main road to the village park. At the entrance, a sign reads "**No overtaking**", because cyclists sometimes race each other and frighten young children. We always walk slowly, so we notice small things. Last week a strong storm blew a large **branch** off the old oak tree, and it now lay across the path. The **leaves** on it were still green, but they were already starting to dry in the sun.

My grandfather is a retired gardener, and he loves explaining how trees live. He pointed to a hole where the **roots** of the oak had been pulled partly out of the **ground**. "A tree cannot drink without its **roots**," he said. "They hold it up, and they also take water from deep under the earth." Then he knelt down on the soft **grass** and touched a tiny **plant** growing between two stones. "Even this little **plant** has found a way to survive," he said with a smile.

I had never thought of a walk as a lesson before. Now I look more carefully every time we go, and I always bring a notebook to record what we see.

passages.title: A Difficult Monday
passages.text:
Last Monday I almost missed my physics presentation. I overslept, grabbed my bag and cycled to school at full speed. At the corner a van suddenly appeared, and I had to **brake** so hard that my pencil case fell open. I was afraid I would **end up** in the principal's office for being late, but I arrived two minutes before the bell.

In the classroom, my **partner**, Linh, was already waiting. We were supposed to present a model of a simple circuit. In my bag I found a **ruler**, a yellow **highlighter pen** and a **rubber**, but my notes were missing. Linh smiled and gave me her copy, and I used the **highlighter pen** to mark the key sentences. Then I used the **ruler** to draw a straight line in my diagram, and the **rubber** to clean a small mistake.

Then our lamp would not turn on. The **plug** was loose, and the wall **socket** was cracked. Our teacher brought another cable, and this time the lamp lit up. The class clapped, and I felt relieved. After the lesson, I promised myself that I would pack my bag the night before, and I thanked Linh for being such a patient **partner**.

passages.title: Studying Together
passages.text:
Our study group meets every Thursday in the library. Last week we were preparing for a geography test, and everyone brought something useful. Hana arrived first and had to **plug in** her laptop, because the battery was almost empty. Then she showed us a map of the region. "We need to **measure** the distance between these two cities," she said, so I decided to **borrow** a ruler from the librarian. She was happy to **lend** me one, and I returned it after ten minutes.

Meanwhile, Tuan was reading a long article about rivers. Whenever he met an unfamiliar word, he would **look up** its meaning in a dictionary. Then he would **highlight** the important sentences so that we could find them again quickly. When I noticed a spelling mistake in my notes, I used a pencil to **rub out** the wrong letters.

At the end, Mai said she would **lend** her excellent notes **to** anyone who needed them, and she even offered to **lend** us her atlas for the weekend. I realised that studying together is not only easier but also more enjoyable, because we share both knowledge and equipment.

passages.title: Mai's First English Lesson
passages.text:
Mai started English classes at a small language school last month, and her first lesson surprised her. The teacher, Mr. Hale, asked everyone to **work with a partner** before speaking to the whole class. Mai's partner, a quiet boy called Tuan, had forgotten his book, so she offered to **share** hers. The room was noisy, so Mr. Hale asked the students at the back to **turn down** their music, while the group by the window was allowed to **turn up** the speaker for a listening task.

During the lesson, learners were encouraged to ask for help. Mai raised her hand and asked, "**What does** 'eager' **mean**?" The teacher explained it with a simple example. Then a boy asked, "**How do you pronounce** 'comfortable'?" and the whole class had to **repeat** the word after him. Mai had been afraid that people would laugh at her mistakes, but Mr. Hale promised to **correct our English** gently and never to make anyone feel embarrassed. By the end of the hour, she felt much braver, and she could not wait for the next class.

passages.title: Learning English Then and Now
passages.text:
Language learning has changed a great deal. **In the past**, students often had to memorise long lists of words and copy grammar rules from the board. **Nowadays**, many classrooms have a friendly **atmosphere** where learners feel free to ask questions. A typical lesson might begin with a student asking, "**How do you spell** 'necessary'?" or "**How do you use the word** 'despite'?" Teachers answer patiently, and they often **explain the difference between** similar words such as 'borrow' **and** 'lend'.

Writing has also become more creative. Instead of copying sentences, learners are asked to **write an essay** about their own lives. My teacher, for example, asked us to describe a neighbour. One classmate wrote that people **call** the old man next door a grumpy dragon, but that he was actually very kind to children. Reading these essays aloud helps everyone see how vocabulary works in real situations. Once learners understand that mistakes are a normal part of learning, they become more confident, more curious and much more willing to try again after every correction.

passages.title: A Relaxed School for English
passages.text:
My cousin Linh studies at an international school with an unusual reputation. The mood there is **relaxed**, and students can **dress** the way they want, as long as they feel comfortable. Teachers use first names, and lessons often take place in the garden. However, the school is very serious about English. In pronunciation class, learners study every **consonant** and **vowel**, listening carefully to how the mouth moves and where the tongue sits. The head teacher says the real goal is to **make yourself understood**, not to sound exactly like a native speaker.

For this reason, students must **be willing to** speak, even when they are not sure of the grammar. They are also encouraged to **experiment with** new expressions instead of repeating the same safe phrases. Linh admits that this was frightening at first. Still, her confidence has grown quickly, and she now talks to visitors without fear. At the end of every term, each student must **take an exam** that tests listening, reading, writing and speaking. Linh believes the friendly rules help her learn faster because she is never nervous or tired of studying.

passages.title: Lan's Second Chance
passages.text:
Every June, thousands of students in my town **do an exam** that decides which university they can join. My cousin Lan was one of them last year. She had always dreamed of being able to **pass an exam** in English with a high score, but the pressure made her very nervous. For two months she planned to **revise for** the test every evening, yet she often felt too tired to concentrate.

On the day itself, Lan did not **do well**. She froze during the listening section, and when the results came out, she learned that she had to **fail an exam** she had studied so hard for. At first she was heartbroken. Her friends were surprised that someone so hardworking could **do badly**, but her teacher explained that one weak result does not define a person.

So in September Lan decided to **retake an exam** at a local centre. This time she slept properly, practised with old papers and stayed calm. Her mother kept saying, "You can only **do your best**, and that is enough." When the second results arrived, Lan had passed with a score she was proud of, and she told everyone that failing once had taught her how to succeed.

passages.title: Two School Systems
passages.text:
My friend Minh spent a year studying in Canada and then moved to a school in Manchester, so he learned how two different systems work. In Canada, his teacher often said, "Just **try your best**, and the results will follow." Students there hope to **get a good grade**, usually an A or a B, while in Manchester pupils want to **get a good mark** out of one hundred.

Minh found both systems demanding. Every weekend he had to **do some revision**, and before the big tests he had to **do exam preparation** with a study group at the library. His weakest skill was writing, so he asked his tutor how to **do an essay** with a clear structure. He also decided to **work on** his vocabulary by reading a news article every morning.

The reading list was enormous at first, but Minh made a timetable and followed it carefully. By December he managed to **get through** all twelve books on the list. Looking back, he says the hardest part was not the content but the habit of studying regularly. He advises younger students to start early. In his opinion, calm planning matters far more than last-minute panic.

passages.title: Inside the Exam Hall
passages.text:
It is eight in the morning, and the exam hall is silent. Each **candidate** sits at a numbered desk with a pencil, an ID card and a worried face. Many of them **find it difficult to** stay calm at this moment, even after months of study.

For most students, the final **grade** matters more than anything else, because it opens the door to a university place. In some schools, however, teachers prefer the word **mark** and give a number instead of a letter.

Behind every good result there is usually **hard work**. Successful students plan their **revision** weeks ahead, review old papers and ask teachers for advice. Good **exam preparation** also includes sleep, healthy food and short breaks, which many young people forget.

Of course, no one can control everything. The questions may be harder than expected, or a nervous mind may forget a simple fact. That is why experienced teachers tell their classes to stay positive. If you have prepared well, then **with a bit of luck** the paper will include topics you know, and you will leave the room smiling. Even a weak result can make the next attempt easier.
